annotations.text:
The audience side is page two.

Open the pages menu in the toolbar and pick "The audience (V2)": onboarding, the Marquee, the session page and the two prompts, the nine beats of the night, the three room layouts, the recap and the Taste Passport.

That page is what a curator's audience actually sees.

Eleven boards, two audiences. The 1J boards are the tools a curator uses to build a screening. Everything else is what her audience sees.

Projector never plays the film. The curator sets a start time, everyone presses play on their own copy, and the notes fire off a shared clock. That is why every film ever made works from day one, with no deal to sign.

Where a curator starts a screening. She names the film and the showtime, then writes the notes that will fire during it.

Research the film and Ask other experts gather material for her. Both come later, so the first build goes straight to Write your notes.

Turning research into notes, and writing one.

A note is a line of text pinned to a moment in the film. The curator types that moment as minutes and seconds, which is the whole of the first build. Later she can drop in a screenshot or describe the scene, and the product finds the moment for her.

Every note for the night in the order it fires, and the screen that starts the show.

To move a note the curator changes its time. Go live counts the curtain down. On zero she presses play on her own television and the clock starts for the whole room.

Hosting, and rehearsing.

On air is what the curator watches during the film: chat, the next note with its countdown, and a button to fire it early.

The dry run plays her whole screening against a clock with nobody watching, so she can catch a mistimed note before an audience ever sees it.
The only two curator screens built for a phone: starting the show, and hosting it. Everything else a curator does happens on a laptop.

What the curator gets once the session is ready, and what she learns afterwards.

Every channel she posts to gets its own link, so she finds out which of them actually fills a room. Nobody else in her life can tell her that.

How someone finds a screening and takes a seat.

Onboarding asks which services they already pay for, so they only see films they can play. The session page is what a shared link opens. A seat is $0.99 and needs an email address, no account.

The beats of a screening, in order.

Doors open half an hour early and the room starts talking. Her other screenings sit under the marquee board, and her own clips fire into the chat on the way to showtime. A countdown runs, then everyone presses play together. Notes arrive while the film runs.

Intermission and falling behind both get their own screen, because both happen on a real night.

The screen you hold during the film. Two states are drawn here: the room before a note arrives, and the moment one does.

Two other layouts sit behind this one, reached by swiping. The full run of notes so far, for rereading. And one note at a time, for anyone who wants the room quiet.

Two screens, both after the credits.

The recap is the record rather than a live surface. The Q&A it holds was answered in the room during the five minutes, in front of the people who asked; this is where it is kept, along with the saved notes and the Film DNA. It is what a link to the evening opens a week later.

Her other screenings sit at the bottom with a reserve action, the same rail that runs in the lobby and during Lights up.

The passport is the audience member's side: what they have sat through, accumulating across all of it.

The five minutes after the film ends.

The house comes up, chat stays open, and the questions people left when they reserved get answered live in front of the people who asked them. Her next screening sits above the compose field, because a reservation taken while the room is still talking converts better than one asked for later.

At minute three a banner carries her live link out to wherever she is continuing. It says where the link goes: TikTok and YouTube resolve to a stream, Instagram only to a profile.

What a link in her bio should open.

Her socials, what she has screened, what is coming with a reserve action, and the things she wants you to see. It is the Taste Passport's mirror: the passport is what you sat through, this is what she programmed.

A session page is the right destination for one screening and the wrong one for a bio, because it dies the morning after. This survives between screenings and books the next one.
